# The hybrid machine-readable REQ format {#sec-format}

A REQ file is Markdown with three layers, each tuned for a different reader.

## Layer 1 — YAML frontmatter (the machine contract)

```yaml
id: REQ-007
title: Group scope — shared access for co-deployed courses
status: open            # draft | open | in-progress | blocked | done | dropped | superseded
kind: feature           # feature | fix | chore | refactor | spec | design | docs
added: 2026-05-26
completed: null
verified_by: null
depends_on: [REQ-005, REQ-006]
backlog_refs: [group-scope]   # backlog items this REQ takes up (REQ-093)
concept_refs: []
scenario_refs: [SCN-002]
supersedes: null
tags: [access]
process:                # optional (REQ-027) — omit when every value is the default
  develop: fused        # fused (default) | split — split = attended design review first
  concept: false        # concept phase (risk buy-down / spike) before develop?
  lab: [REQ-031]        # REQs owning lab assets the System-Test phase requires
```

Validated against `req.schema.json` by `steward lint`. The `id` must match the filename
(`REQ-007.md`). This is the layer the engine reads to build the dependency graph.

The optional **`process:` block** records the intake-time declarations a present human
made: whether develop runs **fused** (one design+build session, the default) or **split**
(an attended design review first, for genuinely risky REQs), whether a **concept phase**
(architecture / risk buy-down / spike — whose deliverable is a `<concepts_dir>/REQ-NNN.md` doc or a
`<concepts_dir>/REQ-NNN/` bundle directory, optionally a committed prototype, REQ-039/REQ-067)
precedes develop, and which REQs own the **lab assets** the
System-Test phase will require. An absent block means exactly the defaults
(`develop: fused`, `concept: false`, `lab: []`); `lab:` references are lint-resolved like
`depends_on`.

## Layer 2 — the acceptance block (the verification contract)

A single fenced block the verifier can run and track. A fully-tagged example showing all
three `check:` values:

````
```yaml acceptance
- id: AC1
  text: The group-token parser grants every child course path in the fixture set.
  test: "pytest tests/test_scope.py::test_group_token_authorizes_children"
  check: regression
  status: pending        # pending | pass | fail  (engine-owned)
- id: AC2
  text: A login against the lab IMAP server fetches the captured mail and the parsed
    fields match the golden copy.
  test: "pytest tests/system/test_imap_fetch.py::test_captured_mail_golden"
  check: artifact
  status: pending
- id: AC3
  text: A reviewer confirms the rendered report is legible and correctly localized.
  test: "manual: reviewer signs off the rendered report"
  check: manual
  status: pending
```
````

Every criterion has an `id`, a human `text`, a runnable `test`, and a **`check:`
classification** — the REQ-027 routing key, validated by `steward lint` on active REQs
(presence + enum only; lint never judges test *quality*):

- **`regression`** — module/unit scope; the oracle is coupled to the code (mock
  assertions); runs headless in the **Build** phase.
- **`live`** (REQ-068) — system scope and a **decoupled** oracle (like `artifact`), but a
  **standing** gate member: the cheapest end-to-end integration proof, run *as* regression
  in **every** develop gate forever, not once-on-demand. This is the matrix cell
  (system-scope × standing) that used to force authors to mislabel an e2e as `regression` or
  hide it behind a pytest marker. A `live` test that **skips** in the develop gate (its
  declared resource absent) is a **hard red**, never a tolerated skip — the engine knows it
  must run.
- **`artifact`** — system scope; a **decoupled, durable** oracle: a captured / golden /
  hashable observable produced by the lab, of which the engine consumes only the
  pass/fail signal. Runs **once** in the **System-Test** phase (a one-time validation).
- **`manual`** — system scope; a **human** oracle; a decision stop inside the
  System-Test phase (a one-time validation).

**One flavor (REQ-068).** Every pytest acceptance command runs as `python -m pytest` under
the one engine-resolved interpreter: a leading bare `pytest …` is normalized to
`<interpreter> -m pytest …` (so the repo root is importable and a `from tests.<helper>`
import resolves). A test never runs in a different *flavor* depending on how a human typed
the string, any more than it runs in a different *lane* depending on a hand-edited marker.

**Degrade — `live → artifact` (REQ-068).** When a newer live proof subsumes an older one,
flip the older AC's `check:` from `live` to `artifact`: it leaves the standing develop gate
and stays re-runnable via `steward revalidate`; record the superseding test/REQ in the AC
text or Notes. Degrade is *reclassification*, not a verb.

**Oracle** (glossary): the part of a test that decides correct vs incorrect — distinct
from the *fixture* (inputs/environment) and the *system under test*. A coupled oracle
(authored alongside the code it checks) cannot disconfirm; what separates the three
`check:` values is the oracle's coupling, not the test's name.

**The environment-bound `regression` smell (REQ-064).** A `regression` whose oracle needs a
service, secret, or network that is absent from a clean repo checkout (a database, a `.env`,
a live service) can only **skip-or-pass** depending on hidden environment — so its green is
*environment-bound*, not self-contained. That is the shape behind the FlowSteward REQ-043
postmortem: an all-`pg_required` AC, filed `regression`, whose green rode a gitignored `.env`,
which then tripped the commit-integrity gate. `/intake` screens every `regression` criterion
for it and routes by oracle coupling: a **decoupled** oracle (a live service / golden output)
is really an `artifact` — reclassify it and name the owning lab REQ in `process.lab`; an oracle
**coupled** to the code that merely needs a **runtime** stays `regression`, with the
required environment recorded in the REQ prose (so the batch lane wires it up). The engine tolerates
such a skip at land (REQ-063), so this is a clarity guardrail, not a ban.

The `status` field is **engine-owned**: the verifier writes `pass`/`fail` back after
running the test. Do not hand-edit it. `steward lint` fails if any active REQ has a
criterion without a test id or without a valid `check:`.

## Layer 3 — prose (the reasoning, untouched)

`## Context`, a `## Decisions` table, the `## Requirement` body, and `## Notes`. This is
where the density that makes a REQ valuable a year later lives. The machine never parses
it; humans always do. Keep it honest about trade-offs and explicit about what is *not* in
scope.

## Why hybrid

Strict schema + parseable blocks give tools exactly what they need; rich prose stays
rich. The schema and linter make the format a **contract, not a convention** — you can't
half-follow it and stay green.

## The backlog — the level above the REQ {#sec-backlog}

A REQ is a **system** requirement: solution-shaped, with criteria naming runnable tests. A
project may also keep the level above it — the need in the *user's* words, which a REQ is
translated from at intake. In ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 terms the backlog is the stakeholder
requirements and a REQ is the system requirements; `/intake` performs the transformation.

The artifact lives at `backlog_file` (default `docs/BACKLOG.md`) and is **honor-when-present**
— a project with no user-need queue keeps none, lints green, and is never nagged about it.
It holds a table and, optionally, the owner's acceptance criteria per item:

```markdown
| Handle | Need | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| rapid-verdict | In a few minutes I can see whether this drive is worth repairing. | operator |

## Acceptance criteria

### rapid-verdict
- In under five minutes I can see whether this drive is worth repairing.
```

A **handle**, not a REQ id: an id in a table reads as a commitment to build that thing, in
that order, and this list commits to nothing. **Origin** is `operator` (their own words) or
`proposed` (a session proposed it, the owner chose it) — the guard against the system writing
its own requirements and then satisfying them.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `steward backlog-add "<need>"` | Record a need. No interview, no schema, no id — the cheap way in. Creates the file if the project has none. |
| `steward backlog-list` | Every item with its **derived** state and attempt record. |
| `steward backlog-accept <handle>` | The owner's verdict: this satisfies the need. |
| `steward backlog-deny <handle> --reason "…"` | It does not. The reason is mandatory. |
| `steward backlog-hold <handle> --reason "…"` | The need stands but is deliberately not being worked. Taking it up lifts the hold. |
| `steward backlog-retire <handle> --reason "…"` | No longer wanted. Nothing is deleted. |

### Two verdicts, and why one of them cannot fail a REQ

A REQ's acceptance criteria are **verification** criteria: did we build what was specified?
They are absolute — a red one fails the REQ. An item's acceptance criteria are the owner's:
was what we specified worth building? That verdict is **advisory to the REQ and blocking to
the item.**

So a REQ can close on green verification while its item is denied — *"exactly as specified"*
and *"still not easy to use"* are both true at once. The REQ stays closed; the item stays
**open**, carrying an attempt record naming the REQ that tried and the reason it did not
land, and any later REQ may take it up. This is Scrum's rule that an unaccepted backlog item
returns to the product backlog rather than reopening the sprint, and it is why acceptance is
a standalone command rather than a step inside the System-Test session: the honest verdict on
something like "easy to use" often arrives only after living with the result.

### Nothing stores status

There is no status column and no "taken up by" column, on purpose. Take-up is recorded once,
in the taking-up REQ's `backlog_refs:`, written by intake in the same commit as the REQ and
its index row. The verdict is recorded once, in the append-only `.devsteward/backlog.jsonl`,
whose *sequence* is the attempt record. Everything an operator reads is derived from those
two at display time — so there is no second copy to fall out of step, and no writer to
forget. `steward lint` checks only that the claims resolve: it never demands that an item be
taken up, ordered, prioritized or ever accepted.

## What is *not* in the REQ

Checkpoint and cursor state. **REQ = spec, ledger = cursor.** The ledger lives in
`.devsteward/`. The only engine-written field inside a REQ is acceptance `status:`.
